title: Learning Isn't Enough
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez challenges the organisational learning orthodoxy: that if teams learn, they improve. Her argument is that learning without the right cultural conditions produces inert knowledge -- people know better but do not do better -- because the social environment does not support the risk of trying new behaviours. Martinez identifies three cultural conditions that must be present before learning translates into changed practice: tolerance for imperfection during skill acquisition (teams must be allowed to perform new behaviours worse before they perform them better); dedicated time for practice distinct from production time; and feedback structures honest enough to be useful rather than diplomatic enough to be comfortable. Drawing on research on skill acquisition, she argues that transfer from knowing to doing is not automatic but requires deliberate practice in conditions that simulate the real application context. Teams that learn in workshops but practice in their actual meetings will transfer skills; teams that return to unchanged meeting structures will not. Martinez's conclusion is addressed to leaders who invest in learning programs without investing in cultural conditions: the program will not work, and the reason is not the content or the facilitator -- it is the environment the learner returns to. Learning is the input; culture is the condition; changed behaviour is the output.
points: Organisational learning without cultural permission for imperfection produces inert knowledge: people know what better looks like but cannot try it without risking social sanction for the period of worse performance that necessarily precedes better performance.

Time for practice is structurally distinct from time for production: teams that learn new behaviours but have no protected time to practice in low-stakes conditions will default to familiar behaviours under production pressure.

Feedback must be honest enough to be useful: diplomatic feedback that preserves comfort while obscuring the gap between current and target performance is validation, not feedback -- and it cannot drive skill acquisition.

The transfer problem is a leadership problem, not a content problem: organisations that invest in learning programs and return learners to unchanged environments demonstrate commitment to the appearance of development, not to development itself.

The sequence that produces changed organisational behaviour: learn + cultural permission for imperfection + dedicated practice time + honest feedback = changed practice; removing any element breaks the causal chain.
quotes: I spend a lot of time thinking about why smart organisations with good intentions keep failing to change how they work, even after they've invested in learning. The answer is almost never the quality of the learning. It's almost always the culture they send people back into.

Learning is the beginning of a process, not the end of one. What you know after a workshop is raw material. What determines whether that raw material becomes changed behaviour is whether the environment you return to gives you permission to be bad at something new long enough to get good at it.

Tolerance for imperfection is not a soft cultural nice-to-have. It is the mechanical precondition for skill acquisition. You cannot get from knowing to doing without passing through a period of doing it badly. Organisations that reward performance above all else punish the transition -- and then wonder why people don't change.

Protected practice time is not a luxury. It is the difference between a learning event and a learning process. Teams that learn in a room and practice in their real meetings will transfer the skill. Teams that learn in a room and return to the same meeting structures they had before will not.

The most common L&D error is investing in the learning and ignoring the conditions. You can have the best content, the most skilled facilitator, the most motivated learners -- and produce nothing, if the environment people return to does not support trying new behaviours under real stakes.

Feedback has to be honest enough to be useful. A feedback culture that preserves relationships at the cost of accuracy is not a feedback culture at all. It is a validation culture with better vocabulary. And validation does not close the gap between current and target performance -- it hides it.
